analysis.one_liner: Toughens federal mine safety enforcement, raises penalties, and protects miners who report hazards.
analysis.headline: The House rejected the mine safety bill 214-193 on December 8, 2010, under a rule that required two-thirds approval, with 213 of 240 voting Democrats in favor and only 1 of 167 voting Republicans.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have tightened enforcement of federal mine safety law after a year of deadly mine disasters: mines with repeated serious violations would have been shut down until they fixed conditions, civil and criminal penalties would have been raised, executives could have been held personally liable, and miners who refused dangerous work or reported hazards would have gained new protections against being fired. It would also have required independent investigations of disasters killing three or more miners and raised the amount of rock dust needed underground to prevent explosions. Brought straight to the House floor with almost no Republican support under a rule requiring a two-thirds majority, it failed 214-193 days before the session ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Miners, especially underground coal miners, and their families. The bill would have let miners refuse work they reasonably believed was dangerous without being fired, paid them full wages for up to 60 days when safety shutdowns idled the mine, given them the right to speak privately with federal investigators without their boss's lawyers present, and raised penalties for operators who retaliate against them. It also would have required mines to brief miners on hazardous conditions before each shift, increased refresher training including a new hour on miners' legal rights, and created a toll-free hotline for reporting hazards [S2] [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Mines with a pattern of recurring serious citations, withdrawal orders, accidents, or injuries would have been placed in 'pattern status,' with an immediate order withdrawing all workers until the operator met remediation requirements, plus eight inspections per year instead of the usual four [S2] [S3].

Civil and criminal penalties would have been raised sharply: repeat criminal violations could draw fines up to $1 million and five years' imprisonment for knowingly violating safety standards, and officers and directors who knowingly authorized violations would face the same civil penalties and fines as the company [S2] [S3].

Miners could not be fired or discriminated against for refusing work they had a good-faith, reasonable belief was a safety or health hazard, and a miner idled by a safety withdrawal order would be entitled to full pay for the entire idled period, up to 60 days, rather than the current one-week limit [S2] [S3].

Any accident killing three or more miners would require an independent investigation panel appointed by the Department of Health and Human Services, chaired by a federal safety research official, to determine causes and make public recommendations; the bill also gave Labor Department investigators subpoena power and the right to interview witnesses privately, without the mine operator's agents or attorneys present [S2] [S3].

The bill would have raised the required incombustible (rock dust) content in underground coal mines from 65 percent to 80 percent, a measure aimed at preventing coal dust explosions, and required atmospheric monitoring systems after NIOSH recommendations [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Coal mine operators. They would have faced doubled civil penalties while in pattern status, fees covering the cost of extra inspections, certification fees, the cost of new atmospheric monitoring and dust-measurement equipment, and the cost of paying miners full wages for up to 60 days during safety shutdowns. Some of those costs could flow through to coal prices and the electricity generated from coal [S2] [S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill imposed real new costs on mine operators: fees to cover additional inspections of mines in pattern status, doubled civil penalties for violations after failing performance benchmarks, mandatory atmospheric monitoring systems and direct-reading dust monitors, and full pay for miners idled up to 60 days by shutdown orders [S2] [S3].

Opponents could fairly argue that some provisions reach beyond safety: the bill would have barred an underground coal mine in pattern status from firing an hourly miner for up to three years without reasonable job-related grounds, an employment protection with only an indirect connection to physical safety, and its design tied a small group of mines' inspection costs to fees charged to those same operators [S3].

An honest supporter would acknowledge that the shutdown-first approach carries economic weight: closing a mine until conditions are remediated idles its workforce and cuts output, and higher compliance and penalty costs in a thin-margin industry could push some marginally profitable mines toward closure, with jobs lost in mining communities even as the rules aim to keep the remaining miners alive [S2] [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade the bill offered was straightforward: higher operating costs and penalties for coal operators in exchange for stronger enforcement of rules whose violation has historically cost miners their lives. The employment protection in Section 117 and the fee-funded inspection scheme are the rougher edges of an otherwise targeted bill, but the main provisions address the specific failures, repeated serious violations and dust buildup, that turn deadly. On the merits, the safety benefits to miners are large and the costs fall on a concentrated industry.

outcome.mechanism: Leaders bypassed committee and brought the bill straight to the House floor under 'suspension of the rules,' a fast-track procedure that requires a two-thirds majority rather than a simple majority; it got 214 votes when it needed 290 and failed, just weeks before that Congress ended [S5] [S6].

narrative.text: Rep. George Miller, the Democratic chairman of the House Education and Labor Committee, introduced the bill on December 3, 2010, and it was referred to his committee [S1] [S5].

Five days later, on December 8, 2010, Miller moved to suspend the rules and pass the bill as amended, skipping a committee markup; consideration under suspension requires the votes of two-thirds of the House [S5].
The vote was postponed and then taken as unfinished business the same day; the motion failed 214-193, with the Yeas and Nays recorded on Roll Call 616 [S5] [S6].
The vote split almost entirely by party: 213 of 240 voting Democrats voted yes and 27 no, while only 1 of 167 voting Republicans voted yes and 166 voted no [S6].
No further action was taken before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal mine operators came out ahead: none of the new penalties, fees, shutdown requirements, personal executive liability, dust standards, or miner pay protections in the bill took effect, and the federal Mine Safety and Health Act of 1977 remained unchanged in this respect.

sides.party_line_note: The vote was almost perfectly partisan: 213 of 240 voting Democrats backed the bill and 27 opposed it, while just 1 of 167 voting Republicans supported it.

industries.note: The bill would have imposed doubled civil penalties, inspection fees, shutdown orders for mines with recurring violations, personal liability for executives who knowingly authorize violations, and up to 60 days' full pay for miners idled by safety shutdowns. Operators' savings from avoiding these rules come at the price of the safety protections the bill was written to guarantee to miners.

industries.industry: Mine safety equipment and monitoring vendors
industries.note: The bill would have required underground coal mines to install atmospheric monitoring systems and use direct-reading dust monitors, creating demand for that equipment. The public benefit runs through the same channel: continuous monitoring of methane, carbon monoxide, and dust levels underground.

industries.industry: Coal-fired electric utilities and coal buyers
industries.note: Stronger enforcement and higher compliance costs could have raised coal prices and electricity costs from coal generation, while safer mines and fewer disaster-driven supply disruptions offer some offsetting value. The effect on consumers would have been modest compared with the bill's effect on operators and miners.
